sugestoes.texto: WHAT: sendAddGuestsEmails receives the raw `guests` input rather than `uniqueGuests`. WHY: an existing attendee who appears in the input is treated as a new guest and gets the 'scheduled' email instead of the 'guests added' notification. HOW: pass `uniqueGuests`.

WHAT: EventManager is built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user), not from the booking organizer. WHY: when an attendee or team admin adds guests, the organizer's calendar event is not updated with the new attendees, and the organizer credentials already loaded in booking.user.credentials are unused. HOW: build the EventManager from the booking owner (booking.user) and its credentials.

WHAT: any attendee, matched by email only, may add an unbounded `guests` array to a booking in any status, with no cap on count. WHY: this lets an attendee use the endpoint as an email relay, because each added guest and every existing attendee and organizer is emailed. HOW: cap the number of guests in the schema (e.g. `.max(10)`), reject cancelled/rejected/past bookings, and consider restricting the permission to the organizer and team admins.
WHAT: the team permission check uses `isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner`. WHY: a team admin who is not an owner is denied if isTeamOwner returns false for them. HOW: combine the two checks with `||`.

WHAT: the guest email is compared as-is against the lowercased blacklist and the stored attendee emails. WHY: a mixed-case guest such as `Bad@X.com` bypasses the blacklist and the duplicate-attendee check. HOW: lowercase the guest before comparing, and compare attendee emails lowercased too.

The blacklist entries are lowercased but the guest email is compared as-is, so a blacklisted address in different case (e.g. Bad@x.com) bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS. Lowercase (and trim) the guest before checking it against the blacklist.

The remove-email tooltip is the hard-coded English string "Remove email", while the rest of this component (e.g. "add_another") goes through t(). Non-English users will see an untranslated tooltip. Use a translation key (add it to the locale file) instead of the literal.

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` joins `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`, so it is true only when the user is both admin and owner. Team admins who are not owners are wrongly denied with FORBIDDEN. The condition should use `||`.

The blacklist entries are lowercased, but the guest email is compared as submitted. A blacklisted address entered with uppercase characters (e.g. `Foo@Bar.com`) bypasses the blacklist. Lowercase the guest before the `includes` check.

`message` is a non-empty template string, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never falls back. The `unable_to_add_guests` string is never shown, and a missing `err.data` yields the literal text "undefined: ...". Build the message conditionally instead.

The error toast renders the raw server `err.message` (and error code) directly. Unexpected backend failures such as Prisma errors from the handler can carry internal details that end up displayed to the user. Only show the message when it is a known translation key, otherwise fall back to the generic `unable_to_add_guests` text.

The blacklist is lowercased but each guest email is compared as typed, so a guest like "Bad@x.com" bypasses a blacklisted "bad@x.com". The duplicate check against existing attendees is also case-sensitive. Normalize guest emails to lowercase before both comparisons.

`message` is a template string that is always truthy, so the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback is dead code. When `err.data?.code` is missing, the toast shows "undefined: ...". Build the message conditionally on the code/message being present.

The attendees are already persisted when `updateCalendarAttendees` runs, and its failure is not handled. A calendar error leaves the DB and calendar out of sync and skips the emails. The user sees an error, and retrying fails because the guests now count as duplicates. Wrap the call in try/catch and log the error so the persisted change still completes (emails still go out), or run the calendar update before the DB write.

The uniqueness check uses a stale read of `booking.attendees` and the write is a plain `createMany`. Two concurrent addGuests calls with the same email both pass the check and insert duplicate attendee rows. Re-check inside a transaction, or rely on a unique constraint, so the same email is not added twice.

The dedup and blacklist comparisons are case-sensitive on the guest side. The blacklist is lowercased but `guest` is not, so `Foo@x.com` bypasses a blacklisted `foo@x.com` and duplicates an existing `foo@x.com` attendee. Normalize each guest to lowercase and compare against lowercased attendee emails.

The handler passes the raw `guests` input to `sendAddGuestsEmails` instead of the filtered `uniqueGuests`. Existing attendees who were re-submitted are then treated as new guests and get the "scheduled" email instead of the "guests added" one. Pass `uniqueGuests`.

The handler passes the raw `guests` input to `sendAddGuestsEmails`, which uses it as the list of newly added attendees. Entries that were filtered out as already-attending are still included. An existing attendee whose address was re-submitted therefore receives the new-booking `AttendeeScheduledEmail` instead of the guests-added notice. Pass `uniqueGuests`, the list actually inserted.

issues.descricao: isTeamAdminOrOwner combines isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner with &&, so only team owners pass; team admins who are not organizer or attendee are wrongly rejected with FORBIDDEN.
issues.textoGolden: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && instead of ||. WHY: isTeamAdmin returns truthy for role ADMIN or OWNER while isTeamOwner returns true only for OWNER, so the && expression is only true for OWNERs; team ADMINs are treated as unauthorized and get FORBIDDEN when adding guests, contradicting the variable's intent. HOW: use `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) || (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0))`.

The flag is named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` but is computed with `&&` (both admin AND owner). A team admin who is not the owner, or the owner who is not flagged admin, will fail this check, so the guard at line 54 wrongly throws FORBIDDEN for legitimate admins/owners. Use `||` between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner.

The variable `isTeamAdminOrOwner` names an OR condition, but the code combines `isTeamAdmin(...)` and `isTeamOwner(...)` with `&&`, so it is true only when the user is both admin AND owner. Either the name is wrong or the operator is; as written the permission check at line 54 denies a plain team admin, contradicting what the identifier promises. Use `||` to match the name (or rename if AND is intended).

issues.descricao: The guest blacklist is lowercased but incoming guest emails are compared without normalization, so a blacklisted address submitted with different casing bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS and is added and emailed.
issues.textoGolden: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The blacklist is compared case-sensitively against guest input while blacklistedGuestEmails are lowercased. WHY: blacklistedGuestEmails entries are lowercased but the filter compares `guest` verbatim (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`); an authenticated user can add a blacklisted address simply by changing its case (e.g. `Foo@bar.com` vs `foo@bar.com`), bypassing the configured BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restriction. HOW: normalize the guest before comparison, e.g. `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())`.

Case-sensitivity bypass of the guest blacklist. `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased on the list side (line 71) but the input side is compared raw: `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` (line 77). A guest email submitted with any different casing (e.g. `Foo@Bar.com` when the blacklist holds `foo@bar.com`) passes the filter and is persisted, defeating BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS. Normalize the input before comparison, e.g. filter on `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())` (and likewise lowercase `guest` for the attendee dedup check).

WHAT: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entries are lowercased but the incoming guest string is compared without lowercasing/normalizing. WHY: an attacker bypasses the blocklist with case variation (e.g. Spam@Example.com) and gets added/emailed.

issues.descricao: The server never deduplicates the guests array, so a request with the same email twice inserts duplicate attendee rows for the booking.
issues.textoGolden: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: uniqueGuests filter only dedupes against existing booking.attendees with case-sensitive === and never dedupes duplicates within the input guests array itself (server schema has no uniqueness refine unlike the client). WHY: a request with the same new email twice creates duplicate attendee rows via createMany.

uniqueGuests filters only against existing attendees/blacklist but never dedupes guests[] itself and schema has no uniqueness check. A request like guests=[a@x.com,a@x.com] passes the filter twice and createMany inserts duplicate attendee rows or throws an unhandled DB unique-constraint exception. Dedupe/normalize input (and reject intra-request duplicates) before createMany.

uniqueGuests filters against existing attendees but does not deduplicate addresses within the incoming guests array. A direct mutation with the same new address twice inserts two Attendee records and sends duplicate invitations because the server schema permits duplicates and the Attendee model has no unique booking/email constraint. Deduplicate normalized input before filtering and inserting.

issues.descricao: Check-then-insert without a transaction or unique constraint lets two concurrent addGuests calls for the same email both pass the existing-attendee check and create duplicate attendees.

comentarios.texto: Race condition: findFirst check for existing attendees then booking.update+createMany is not atomic. Two concurrent addGuests calls with the same new email both see it as absent and both insert, creating duplicates. Guard with a unique constraint and handle conflict or run in a transaction/serializable check.

Check-then-insert race: the handler reads `booking.attendees` at the start, filters against it, then inserts in a separate `prisma.booking.update ... createMany` with no transaction or unique guard. Two concurrent addGuests calls for the same guest both see it as absent and both insert, producing duplicate attendees. Wrap the read+filter+insert in a transaction (or rely on a unique constraint on (bookingId, email) and handle the conflict) so concurrent requests cannot both succeed.

issues.descricao: Attendee authorization and existing-attendee dedup compare emails case-sensitively, so an attendee with differently-cased stored email is FORBIDDEN and a case-variant of an existing attendee is added again.

comentarios.texto: Inconsistent email normalization for identity checks. Both the authorization check `attendee.email === user.email` (line 52) and the existing-attendee dedup `guest === attendee.email` (line 76) use strict case-sensitive equality, while emails are treated as case-insensitive everywhere else in this handler (the blacklist block directly below lowercases). Consequence: a legitimate attendee whose stored casing differs from their session email is wrongly FORBIDDEN, and a guest differing from an existing attendee only by case is duplicated rather than filtered. Compare on a normalized form (both sides `.toLowerCase()`), consistent with the blacklist normalization.

issues.descricao: The handler passes the unfiltered guests list to sendAddGuestsEmails, which uses it to pick who gets AttendeeScheduledEmail, so existing attendees included in the request receive a new-booking confirmation instead of the add-guests email.
issues.textoGolden: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) passes the raw input guests instead of the filtered uniqueGuests. WHY: already-existing attendees included in the request are misclassified as newGuests in email-manager and receive AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail (wrong notification).

Dead-transform / wrong input: `uniqueGuests` is computed (dedup vs existing attendees + blacklist) and written to DB, but `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the original `guests`. Existing attendees re-submitted are then `includes()`-matched as new and get AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. Pass `uniqueGuests`.

Pass `uniqueGuests` (the filtered set written to DB) to sendAddGuestsEmails instead of raw `guests`; the email layer assumes newGuests exactly equals newly created attendees for its Scheduled vs AddGuests branch.

issues.descricao: EventManager is created with the requesting user's credentials, so when a non-organizer adds guests the organizer's calendar event is not updated (or the wrong account is used) for references without a credentialId.

comentarios.texto: EventManager is initialized with the requesting user's credentials rather than the booking organizer's credentials. When an attendee or team owner adds guests to a booking whose calendar reference lacks credentialId, updateAllCalendarEvents selects credentials by type from the caller's calendars, so the organizer's event is not updated or the update targets the wrong account. Load credentials for booking.userId and initialize the manager with the booking owner.

issues.descricao: Claims a failing calendar update at addGuests.handler.ts:165 aborts the mutation after guests are persisted; the calendar update path already swallows provider errors.

comentarios.texto: The attendees are written to the database at line 92, but `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` at line 165 runs outside the try/catch. If it throws, the mutation returns an error even though the guests are already persisted, so the DB and the calendar are out of sync. No emails are sent, and a retry then fails with 'emails_must_be_unique_valid'. Catch and handle the calendar update failure after the DB write.

The attendees are already committed to the DB when `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` is awaited without a try/catch. If the calendar sync throws, the mutation returns an error and skips the emails, although the guests were added. The caller sees a failure for a partly applied change and may retry. Handle calendar sync failure as best-effort, as the email send is, or run it before the DB write.

issues.descricao: Claims any attendee can add guests and trigger invites; this is the deliberate permission model of the new feature.

comentarios.texto: Any attendee, matched only by email, is allowed to add arbitrary guests to a booking, and the handler then sends emails and calendar invites on the organizer's behalf. Any attendee can use this to send invites to arbitrary addresses. Restrict the action to the organizer and team admins, or verify that the attendee's email is confirmed.

issues.descricao: The guests array has no server-side size limit, so any authorized caller, including an attendee, can add thousands of guests and trigger an unbounded batch of inserts and emails.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: guests is an unbounded z.array(z.string().email()) with no max length. WHY: any authorized caller (including a mere attendee) can submit thousands of emails causing unbounded createMany inserts plus unbounded Promise.all email fanout in sendAddGuestsEmails.

The mutation accepts an unbounded guest array that is persisted and immediately expanded into concurrent emails to every attendee. For non-seated bookings each email's ICS serializes the full attendee list, so adding N guests creates O(N) concurrent sends and O(N²) aggregate attachment work; repeated additions also resend to all existing attendees. Enforce a server-side guest-count and total-attendee limit before insertion and bound notification concurrency.

issues.descricao: The Remove email tooltip in MultiEmail is a hard-coded English string instead of a translation key.

comentarios.texto: Tooltip content="Remove email" is hard-coded English user-facing text bypassing i18n while surrounding strings in the same file/PR use t(). Wrap it in t() e.g. content={t("remove_email")} and add the key to locales.

`Tooltip content="Remove email"` is a hard-coded English user-facing string, while the surrounding code in this same component routes user text through `t()` (e.g. `t("add_another")` on line 69). This string bypasses the translation mechanism and will never be localised; it should use a translation key.

The new removal tooltip hard-codes `Remove email`, so users in non-English locales see English text even though the neighbouring controls use `t(...)` and this component already obtains `t` from useLocale. Route this tooltip through a translation key (and supply its English translation) rather than using the literal.

issues.descricao: The onError fallback to unable_to_add_guests is unreachable because the template-string message is always truthy.

comentarios.texto: Unreachable fallback: `message` is a template string `${code}: ${...}` which is always truthy, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never takes the fallback. Build message conditionally or test the underlying parts for emptiness.

In `onError`, `message` is always a non-empty template string (`"${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}"`), so the fallback `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` is unreachable and the newly added `unable_to_add_guests` translation is never shown. The user is instead shown a raw error code prefix like `BAD_REQUEST: ...` rather than the translated message; the fallback and code prefix handling should be corrected so the intended translated text reaches the user.

The error message is built as a template string, so it is always truthy. The `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback is therefore dead code, and the user can see "undefined: ..." or an untranslated raw message. Use `err.message ? t(err.message) : t("unable_to_add_guests")`.

issues.descricao: After a validation failure followed by a successful add, isInvalidEmail stays true, so the stale emails_must_be_unique_valid error shows the next time the dialog is opened.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: addGuestsMutation onSuccess resets multiEmailValue and closes the dialog but never resets isInvalidEmail. WHY: after one failed validation the red emails_must_be_unique_valid error persists on the next open/successful add.

issues.descricao: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the event type's disableStandardEmails settings, so hosts and attendees receive add-guests emails even when standard emails are disabled.
issues.textoGolden: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

issues.descricao: The add-guests handler omits booking.iCalUID from the CalendarEvent, so the add-guests emails' .ics attachments use booking.uid as UID and recipients' calendars treat them as a new event rather than an update of the original booking invite.
The addGuests FORBIDDEN error uses the translation key you_do_not_have_permission, which is missing from the locale files, so the dialog shows the raw key to users.
The comment in MultiEmailLazy.tsx ("These are like 40kb") is copied from the phone input lazy loader and does not apply to MultiEmail, which only uses existing UI components.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator but copies the numeric Paginator's get_item_key/value_from_cursor, instead of DateTimePaginator's datetime-aware versions. WHY: the audit log endpoint orders by the datetime field, so math.ceil/floor(datetime) raises TypeError in build_cursor, and a raw numeric cursor value is compared against a datetime column. Every request with optimized_pagination=true therefore fails with a 500 or a wrong query. HOW: subclass DateTimePaginator, or reuse its get_item_key and value_from_cursor.

WHAT: the advanced-features branch slices the queryset with a negative start offset (queryset[cursor.offset:stop]). WHY: Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise AssertionError, so a client-supplied cursor with a negative offset causes a 500. This also contradicts the comment that the ORM handles it. HOW: reject or clamp negative offsets (raise BadPaginationError or use max(0, offset)) and remove the negative-offset branch.

WHAT: BasePaginator clamps negative offsets only when cursor.is_prev is false, and passes negative offsets through unchanged when is_prev is true. WHY: with a prev cursor and a negative offset, queryset[negative:stop] raises AssertionError (500), and the non-prev clamp silently changes the existing behavior for all paginators. HOW: validate offset >= 0 for both directions and raise BadPaginationError, rather than conditionally clamping.

The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`). Django querysets raise AssertionError on negative indexing, so a crafted cursor with a negative offset causes a 500 for admins using `optimized_pagination=true`. Even where negative slicing is supported, `stop = start + limit + extra` would give a wrong window. Clamp the offset to a non-negative value, or reject negative offsets, instead of passing them to the slice.

The new branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`) when a user-supplied cursor has a negative offset. Django raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') for negative slice bounds, so the request fails with an unhandled 500. Remove this branch, or reject or clamp negative offsets with a 400 before slicing.

OptimizedCursorPaginator uses Paginator's numeric get_item_key/value_from_cursor, but the audit-log endpoint paginates on the DateTimeField "datetime". math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError for any non-empty page, and the raw cursor value is never converted back to a datetime. Subclass DateTimePaginator, or copy its multiplier-based get_item_key and value_from_cursor.

The comments claim the Django ORM handles negative slicing and that this is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level. Both are false. Django QuerySets raise AssertionError on a negative slice start, and the queryset filter is by organization, not by pagination bounds. The comments describe behavior that does not exist, so remove or correct them to say negative offsets are unsupported.

The comment says negative offsets are allowed and that the queryset handles boundary conditions. The code clamps only when `not cursor.is_prev`, and a negative offset still reaches the queryset slice when `is_prev` is true. Django does not handle that, so the comment is untrue. Rewrite it to describe the actual clamp.

The OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring advertises negative offset support, streamlined boundary handling and an optimized query path. The implementation is a copy of BasePaginator.get_result, issues the same sliced query, and a negative slice fails in Django. The docstring misdescribes the class. Align it with what the class does.

OptimizedCursorPaginator overrides get_item_key and value_from_cursor with generic numeric versions (math.floor on the raw attribute, and cursor.value returned as-is). The audit-log endpoint paginates on a datetime field. With ?optimized_pagination=true, math.floor(datetime) will raise TypeError, and the cursor value will not be converted back to a datetime for filtering. Subclass DateTimePaginator, or reuse its datetime-to-timestamp key conversion and cursor-value conversion.

The comment says the Django ORM handles negative slicing, but Django querysets raise on negative indexes ("Negative indexing is not supported"). A cursor with a negative offset therefore produces a 500 instead of the claimed 'advanced' pagination. The result also contradicts the code, because the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check later uses `offset` while the slice used `start_offset`. Reject negative offsets with a BadPaginationError, or clamp them to 0.

The comment says negative offsets are allowed because the queryset handles boundaries. The code only clamps non-prev offsets to 0 and still passes a negative offset through for is_prev cursors, which fails in the ORM. This also changes the behaviour of BasePaginator for every endpoint without delivering the stated feature. Revert this hunk to the original `stop = offset + limit + extra; queryset[offset:stop]`.

The 'advanced' path passes a negative cursor offset straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django querysets reject negative indexing (AssertionError), so any request with a negative cursor offset and `optimized_pagination=true` returns a 500. The Cursor contract was loosened to allow negative offsets, but the ORM slicing consumer was not updated to match. Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError, or translate them into a valid ordered query, instead of slicing with them.

BasePaginator.get_result now clamps negative non-prev offsets to 0 and lets negative prev offsets through to the slice. Previously a negative offset was never silently accepted, so every paginator inheriting this code now returns the first page for a bad cursor. For is_prev cursors it still reaches Django's unsupported negative slice. The later `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check still uses the unclamped offset, so it no longer matches the slice that was actually executed. Restore the original `queryset[offset:stop]` behavior and reject negative offsets explicitly.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative cursor offsets straight into Django queryset slicing, which Django does not support, so requests with a negative offset raise an error instead of returning a page.
issues.textoGolden: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

comentarios.texto: The advanced negative-offset branch passes a negative slice start directly to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative indexing. A cursor such as 0:-1:0 is accepted by Cursor.from_string but crashes the optimized audit-log request instead of providing reverse pagination. Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError or implement reverse traversal using nonnegative slices and reversed ordering.

The comment claiming that Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false: Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices. This branch passes cursor.offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], so it raises rather than supplying the documented negative-offset pagination. Correct the negative-offset support claims here, in the class docstring, and in the new BasePaginator boundary-handling comment (or implement actual supported boundary handling) so callers are not promised a pagination mode that the underlying queryset cannot provide.

Django QuerySets do not support negative slice bounds. Passing a negative cursor offset directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` raises an exception instead of enabling advanced pagination. Validate or normalize negative offsets before slicing, or implement reverse traversal through ordering/filtering rather than negative slices.

issues.descricao: The comment added to BasePaginator claims negative offsets are allowed and safely handled by the queryset, but the code clamps non-prev offsets to zero and leaves prev offsets as before, so the comment misdescribes the behaviour.

comentarios.texto: The added comment says this change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination ... safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the statement it annotates, line 182, is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` — it clamps negative offsets to 0, i.e. it does the opposite of what the comment claims and leaves the 'negative offset' (offset < 0) paging behaviour exactly as before. The comment is now untrue for the code it sits on; either drop the 'allow negative offsets' wording or make the code actually permit them.

The comment declares this change `allow[s] negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination`, but the actual computation is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which clamps non-prev offsets at 0 — i.e. it never permits a negative offset. The declared optimization is a no-op relative to the original `queryset[offset:stop]`; the comment describes behavior the code does not have.

BasePaginator now passes the raw `offset` to the slice whenever `cursor.is_prev` is true (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). A negative offset from a user-supplied prev cursor therefore reaches `queryset[negative:stop]`, which Django rejects. This crashes every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. Fix: always use `max(0, offset)`, or validate the offset when the cursor is parsed.

issues.descricao: The OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring claims streamlined boundary handling, an optimized query path and backward compatibility that the implementation, a copy of BasePaginator plus a negative-offset branch, does not provide.

comentarios.texto: Docstring lists 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets', and 'maintaining backward compatibility', but get_result (845-886) is a copy of BasePaginator with only a negative-offset branch added — no streamlined handling or optimized path exists, and negative-offset slicing breaks prior cursor semantics. Doc describes behavior the function does not produce — align doc to code or implement the claimed handling.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator computes cursor keys with math.floor/ceil on the raw attribute, but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so building the cursor raises TypeError for any non-empty result.
issues.textoGolden: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

comentarios.texto: OptimizedCursorPaginator requires numeric integer keys (get_item_key uses math.floor/ceil + int, cursor_value defaults to 0) but is instantiated here with order_by="-datetime". This mismatched producer/consumer contract breaks pagination for datetime-ordered audit logs. Fix: do not use OptimizedCursorPaginator for datetime ordering; keep DateTimePaginator or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key/value_from_cursor mishandles datetime ordering by calling math.floor/ceil directly on a datetime and returning raw int cursor value. WHY: Used with order_by="-datetime" it crashes with TypeError on floor(datetime) when building cursors and filters the datetime column against an int in build_queryset, breaking pagination. HOW: Copy DateTimePaginator logic — timestamp via strftime/multiplier with floor/ceil and convert cursor value back with datetime.fromtimestamp.

The optimized branch selects a numeric-key paginator while ordering by the datetime field. On any nonempty first page, build_cursor invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, which calls math.ceil on a datetime and raises TypeError; nonzero cursors also lack the datetime conversion provided by DateTimePaginator. Make the optimized paginator inherit DateTimePaginator or preserve its timestamp encoding and decoding.

issues.descricao: The audit log endpoint always dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access, which crashes with AttributeError for authorized token requests that have no member, even on the default pagination path.
issues.textoGolden: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

comentarios.texto: The unconditional advanced-access check dereferences organization_context.member although RpcUserOrganizationContext permits member=None. sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `totalPages` is computed as `floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which over-counts by one when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`. WHY: with 50 members and limit 50 it shows 1/2, `showingLast` stays false on the real last page, and `next` loads an empty page. HOW: use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`.

WHAT: `add_members` calls `group.add(user)` for every submitted username without checking whether the user is already a member. WHY: `group_users` has a unique index on (group_id, user_id), so adding an existing member raises RecordNotUnique and returns a 500. The previous `usernames=` implementation only added `expected - current`. HOW: skip users who are already members, for example `group.add(user) unless group.users.exists?(user.id)`.

WHAT: the `members` action uses a client-supplied `limit` with no upper bound, and the old 200 default cap for automatic groups was removed. WHY: a request such as `limit=1000000` loads and serializes every member of a large group in one request, and a negative or zero limit errors or breaks the client page math. HOW: clamp it, for example `limit = [[(params[:limit] || 50).to_i, 1].max, 200].min`, and use `[params[:offset].to_i, 0].max` for the offset.

totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which over-counts by one whenever user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 members with limit 50 gives 2 pages). showingLast is then false on the real last page, so 'next' fetches an empty page (offset == user_count) and the UI shows a nonexistent page. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit).

This happens when two admins remove the same member, or on a stale member list, and it returns a 500/404 instead of succeeding silently. Look the user up first and delete it only if it is present in the group.

`totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which over-counts by one whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with limit 50 yields 2 pages instead of 1). Since `showingLast` is `propertyEqual("currentPage", "totalPages")`, on a full last page `showingLast` is false, so the `next` action stays enabled and advances `offset` to `user_count`, rendering an empty page labeled as the last page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the zero-member guard) so the count matches the real number of pages.

issues.descricao: The mock occurrence builder ignores its value argument, so tests (e.g. group_2 expected with 6 while the packet carries 10) pass regardless of which value is passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data.
issues.textoGolden: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

comentarios.texto: The new occurrence builder accepts `value` but never incorporates or asserts it, so the occurrence tests cannot detect incorrect forwarding of the measured value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. For example, `test_state_results_multi_group` supplies 10 for group_2 but builds its expected occurrence with 6 and still passes. A regression that passes a constant or another group's measurement at the new production hook would therefore go unnoticed. Include the value in the mock occurrence's evidence and use the actual expected measurement, or assert the hook's arguments directly.

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value: int` but never uses it (the occurrence is built only from `group_key`/`new_status`), and this same helper is also the implementation of `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because neither the expected occurrence nor the handler output depends on the value, tests like `test_state_results_multi_group` (which incorrectly builds the group_2 occurrence with `value=6` while the packet carries `10`) and `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` (expected built with 6 vs packet 8) pass regardless of the value actually passed into `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. If evaluation passed a wrong value, these tests would still pass, so they do not verify the value/threshold path they appear to cover. Include `value` in a field of the occurrence (or assert on it in the handler) and fix the wrong expected values so the argument is actually checked.

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts a `value: int` parameter but never uses it — the returned IssueOccurrence is derived only from `group_key` and `new_status`. Because `value` is dead, callers can pass a mismatched value with no failure: in `test_state_results_multi_group` the packet contains `group_2: 10`, but the expected occurrence for `group_2` is built with `6`. Either use `value` when constructing the occurrence so the test validates the group value, or drop the unused parameter and pass the correct value; otherwise the test silently accepts wrong group values.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `_get_event_stats` passes the outer `dataset` variable to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` instead of its own `scoped_dataset` parameter. WHY: the dashboard-widget split path calls `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` with a rewritten query and a different dataset. The upsampling decision is then made from the wrong dataset (for example metrics or transactions), so errors are not upsampled, or the transform is applied to a dataset that was not queried. HOW: pass `scoped_dataset`, and make the discover check use the `query` argument rather than `request.GET['query']`.

WHAT: `_is_error_focused_query` decides with the substring check `'event.type:error' in query`. WHY: a negated or compound query such as `!event.type:error` or `event.type:error_foo` matches, so the discover query gets `upsampled_count()` (sum of `sample_weight`) even though it does not target error events. That produces wrong counts, or a failed query if the column is missing in the queried table. HOW: parse the query with the search parser, or at least use a token-boundary regex that rejects a leading `!` or a trailing word character.
The truthiness check `if client_sample_rate:` treats a present but falsy value (0 or 0.0) as missing, so `sample_rate` is silently not set. Use an explicit `is not None` check instead.

The upsampling decision is computed from the outer `dataset`, but the query runs against the `scoped_dataset` parameter of `_get_event_stats`. When the two differ, `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` for a dataset that was not checked, or the rewrite is skipped for one that should have it. Pass `scoped_dataset` to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`.

`_is_error_focused_query` uses a raw substring check, so `!event.type:error`, `event.type:[error,default]` or `event.type:transaction OR event.type:error` also match. That makes the discover dataset rewrite count() to `upsampled_count()` (sum of `sample_weight`) for queries that return transactions, which have no such column, so the Snuba query fails. Parse the query's search filters and apply the transform only for a positive, exact `event.type:error` filter with no negation or OR.

The inline comments say each bucket has 1 event, but the assertions expect count == 10. The 10 is the upsampled value (1 event at client_sample_rate 0.1), so the comments contradict the assertions. Update them to say that one stored event is upsampled to 10.

The transaction event is stored without a client sample rate, so its weight is 1. Upsampled and plain counts are therefore identical (1 and 0), and the test passes even if transactions were wrongly upsampled. Give the transaction a sample rate such as 0.1 in its data, or add an error event that should be excluded, so a wrongly applied upsample would produce 10 and fail the assertion.

issues.descricao: The upsampling decision is evaluated against the request's dataset instead of the scoped_dataset actually queried, so in the dashboard discover-split path (metrics dataset) error queries run against discover skip upsampling even when all projects are allowlisted.
issues.textoGolden: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

comentarios.texto: The upsampling decision uses the closure variable `dataset` while the transformed `final_columns` are executed against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-split path `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` at lines 351, 365, 406, 423) than the request's `dataset`, so the `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` branch can be evaluated against the wrong dataset and apply/skip `sum(sample_weight)` for a dataset that was never queried. Base the decision on the dataset actually being queried (`scoped_dataset`) so the transform matches the target of the query.

issues.descricao: _is_error_focused_query uses a substring match for `event.type:error` on the request query, so negated or mixed (OR transaction) discover queries are treated as error-only and get the sample_weight sum instead of count().

comentarios.texto: `_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to apply `upsampled_count()` by doing a naive substring search for `event.type:error` in the raw request query. A query that excludes errors (e.g. `!event.type:error`) or the discover-split query `({query}) AND event.type:transaction` still contains the literal `event.type:error`, so the transform is applied to a non-error / transactions query, summing `sample_weight` where it should be a plain `count()` and producing wrong bucket values. It also ignores the actual `query` passed to `_get_event_stats`, so the decision can differ from the query that is really executed. Match on a parsed/negation-aware condition (or pass the resolved query string) instead of a raw substring test.

The substring check treats `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` as error-only queries. For allowlisted projects this rewrites count() to an aggregation over sample_weight even when the Discover query includes transactions, violating the error-only restriction and potentially failing against a transaction-backed query. Determine the event-type restriction from the parsed query rather than the presence of a substring.

Substring matching does not establish that the Discover query selects only errors. For example, `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both return True here, causing count() to be replaced with the sample-weight aggregation for non-error or mixed results in allowlisted projects. This contradicts the error-only guard and can produce incorrect counts. Parse the query and establish an error-only restriction (including negation and Boolean structure), or conservatively skip transformation when that restriction cannot be proven.

issues.descricao: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot detect upsampling being applied to transaction queries, because the transaction has no sample_weight and upsampled_count() equals count() for it.

comentarios.texto: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events would still pass if upsampling were wrongly applied to transaction queries. The transaction event has no sample_weight, and upsampled_count uses ifNull(sample_weight, 1), so the result is still 1 and 0. Give the transaction a non-default sample rate or weight so an upsampled count would differ from a plain count, or assert that the transform was not applied.

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot falsify over-application of upsampling: the stored transaction has no sample_weight so upsampled_count() (sum(ifNull(sample_weight,1))) returns 1, same as count(). Give the transaction a sample_weight/client_sample_rate that would diverge (e.g. count 10 if upsampled vs 1 if not), or assert via mock that transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling was not called / yAxes were not rewritten.

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot detect upsampling being wrongly applied to transaction queries. The stored transaction event has no error_sampling context, so sample_weight is null, and upsampled_count = toInt64(sum(ifNull(sample_weight,1))) evaluates to 1 for it — identical to count(). If _should_apply_sample_weight_transform/_is_error_focused_query were broken so that a discover query with event.type:transaction gets upsampled, the assertion count==1 (and 0 in the empty bucket) would still pass. Add an event with a known non-1 sample_weight (or assert the emitted query uses count() and not upsampled_count) so the test actually fails when the transaction exclusion is bypassed.

issues.descricao: The test factory helper's docstring promises a valid client sample rate but it copies any truthy float-convertible value (negative, >1, strings), unlike production validation.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling uses `if client_sample_rate: float(...)` with no type/range check, unlike production _derive_client_error_sampling_rate which requires isinstance(int,float) and 0<rate<=1. WHY: string '0.1', bool True, or out-of-range 5.0 get stored as sample_rate in fixtures while production drops them, making upsampling tests diverge from prod. HOW: mirror production validation before assigning sample_rate.

The new docstring says the client sample rate must be 'present and valid', but the implementation only checks truthiness and float conversion. Negative rates, rates greater than 1, and float-convertible non-finite values are all accepted and written to sample_rate. This falsely tells test authors that this helper enforces sample-rate validity. Either document that it merely copies truthy float-convertible values, or validate the supported sample-rate range and finiteness before setting the field.

issues.descricao: With upsampling active, top-events queries pick and order the top N groups by raw count() (selected_columns/orderby are not transformed) while the plotted series use upsampled_count(), so ranking can disagree with the displayed weighted counts.

comentarios.texto: Only timeseries_columns are upsampled while selected_columns and orderby used to select the Top N remain based on raw count(). discover.top_events_timeseries first queries those unchanged selected columns to choose groups, so a group with fewer retained events but a higher weighted count is omitted in favor of a lower-volume group. Apply the weighted-count transformation consistently to Top N selection and its ordering as well as the displayed timeseries.

issues.descricao: _are_all_projects_error_upsampled and its caller take an organization argument that is never read.

comentarios.texto: `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` takes an `organization` argument — also threaded in from the public `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — but never reads it: the body uses only `project_ids` and the global option `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. The declared parameter is dead. Either the allowlist check is meant to be organization-scoped (the body must actually consult `organization`) or the parameter should be removed from both functions; as written the signature advertises an organization-scoped decision the implementation never makes.

issues.descricao: Claims only bare count() is rewritten, so aliased count, eps(), epm(), count_unique() etc. stay un-upsampled.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only rewrites exact bare `count()` and passes everything else through unchanged. WHY: yAxes like `count() as foo`, `eps()`, `epm()`, `count_unique()`, `count_if()` keep raw counts while should_upsample is true, returning under-counted timeseries. HOW: parse/normalize the function (strip alias, match function name with args) and rewrite all count-equivalent aggs or explicitly fall back to no-upsampling.

issues.descricao: Rewriting count() to `upsampled_count() as count` breaks responses for transformAliasToInputFormat=1: the result column is translated to the rewritten field string while the serializer still reads `count()`.

comentarios.texto: Replacing count() with `upsampled_count() as count` breaks requests using transformAliasToInputFormat=1. QueryBuilder.process_results translates the count alias to the replacement field string, but the endpoint serializer still resolves the original axis as `count()`, so it cannot read the weighted count from the returned rows. Preserve the original public field name in the result mapping when rewriting the internal aggregation.

issues.descricao: upsampled_count truncates the weighted sum with toInt64 instead of rounding, under-counting the estimate by up to one per bucket.

comentarios.texto: `upsampled_count` wraps the sum in `toInt64`, which truncates toward zero: `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` of e.g. 1.5 or 3.33 yields 1 or 3 instead of the nearest integer, systematically under-counting the upsampled estimate (worst when weights are just below an integer). Use a rounding aggregation (e.g. `toInt64(round(sum(...)))`) so the reconstructed count reflects the intended estimate rather than a floored value.

issues.descricao: The 'no project IDs' test case runs with an empty allowlist mock, so it passes via the empty-allowlist branch and does not verify the empty project_ids guard.

comentarios.texto: The 'no project IDs provided' case does not exercise the `if not project_ids: return False` guard. mock_options.get.return_value was set to [] just above (line 48), so removing the project_ids guard still returns False via the `if not allowlist` branch, and this assertion passes either way. Re-mock options.get to return a non-empty allowlist (e.g. self.project_ids) before calling with project_ids=[], so the empty-project guard is actually falsifiable.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is read with a hard subscript, so a span missing the field raises KeyError. WHY: the exception propagates out of process_batch, which fails the whole batch and blocks offset commits. The consumer then crash-loops on the poison message. The `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` call does no runtime validation. HOW: use `.get()` with a fallback, or skip and count spans that lack the field.

WHAT: zunionstore uses the default AGGREGATE SUM when merging sets. WHY: a payload present in both sets, for example after a redelivered span, gets its score added to itself. That corrupts the end-timestamp ordering, so eviction can keep the wrong spans. HOW: pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to both zunionstore calls.

The `max_segment_spans` constructor option (default 1001) is still declared and stored, but this PR removed the only code that read it. The span limit is now a hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Changing `max_segment_spans` therefore has no effect, and the Python default (1001) disagrees with the Lua constant (1000). Either pass the limit into the Lua script as an ARGV value, or remove the unused option so the two cannot diverge.

The module docstring and key glossary still describe `span-buf:s:*` as plain sets and say the payload is simply added to the set. After this change the keys are sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and `add-buffer.lua` trims each one to 1000 spans, popping the lowest scores. Update the docstring to say sorted sets, the score, and the 1000-span cap.

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is a hard key lookup, and the `cast` to SpanEvent does no runtime validation. A span message without the field raises KeyError in process_batch, and the consumer crashes and replays that poison message. Read it defensively, for example by falling back to the message timestamp or skipping the span.

The script and `zscan` now treat `span-buf:s:*` keys as sorted sets. Segment keys already in Redis from before the deploy are plain SETs. `zcard`, `zunionstore` and `zscan` on them raise WRONGTYPE, which aborts the EVALSHA pipeline and the flush until the old keys expire. Use a new key prefix or version for the zset buffer, or drain the old keys before rollout.

issues.descricao: ZUNIONSTORE merges sorted sets with the default SUM aggregate, so a span payload present in both keys gets a doubled end-timestamp score and is wrongly kept by the oldest-first eviction.

comentarios.texto: ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so when the same span payload is present in both `set_key` and the merged `span_key`/`parent_key` (duplicate delivery is anticipated by this buffer's own comments), its score is added instead of being kept equal to `end_timestamp_precise`. Because eviction at line 63 (`zpopmin` by score) compares scores across all members of `set_key`, a summed score makes the duplicated span appear far newer than its real end timestamp and biases eviction away from legitimately-old spans, breaking the stated 'evict oldest end timestamps' contract. Use ZUNIONSTORE ... AGGREGATE MIN (or MAX) so a duplicate keeps a single end timestamp score rather than doubling it.

ZUNIONSTORE uses its default SUM aggregation, so replayed payloads present in both the temporary parent_key and the resolved set_key receive the sum of their end timestamps. Replaying a child whose parent already redirects to an ancestor therefore makes that old span score roughly twice its actual timestamp, protecting it from eviction over genuinely newer spans. Use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN for identical timestamp scores) on both union operations to preserve timestamp scores when members overlap.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both the destination and source has its timestamp doubled rather than preserved. This can happen when a previously merged span is replayed into its original subtree key. The duplicated span then sorts after genuinely newer spans and survives ZPOPMIN eviction incorrectly. Specify AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, since identical payloads should have identical timestamps) on both union calls so merging remains idempotent and scores remain end timestamps.

issues.descricao: Segment keys change from Redis sets to sorted sets under the same key names, so keys left by the previous release make ZADD, ZCARD and ZSCAN fail with WRONGTYPE during rollout, crashing span processing and flushing.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Changed SET ops (scard/sunionstore) to ZSET ops (zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin) with no migration breaks in-flight segments. WHY: Old keys of type SET still live up to TTL; ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN/ZADD on the opposite type raises WRONGTYPE and fails inserts/flushes during rollout.

The segment keys were migrated from Redis SETs to SORTED SETs (ZADD/ZSCAN/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN), but nothing handles the keys written by the currently deployed release. During a rolling deploy, an existing `span-buf:s:{...}:{id}` key is still a SET, so this `p.zadd(...)` (and the flusher's `p.zscan(...)`, and the Lua `zcard`/`zunionstore`) raises WRONGTYPE 'Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value'. That exception is unhandled: it aborts the whole pipeline/Lua invocation and crashes the consumer batch. Add a key-schema version to the key name (or a migration/fallback) so old SET-typed keys cannot be touched as sorted sets.

The new ZADD writes sorted sets into the same span-buf:s namespace previously populated by SADD, without migrating existing set keys. The new bound relies entirely on insert-time eviction in the Lua script; if that eviction fails to bound a key (e.g. duplicated/scored members or the concurrent-writer case the code itself warns about at lines 457-461), this method will now materialize an unbounded number of spans into memory and emit them, whereas before it was safely skipped. Re-introduce a span-count guard (or verify the invite-time eviction strictly caps cardinality) to keep memory bounded.

buffer.py declares the segment span limit as the configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001, line 150) and this hunk removed the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` size guard from the flush path, while the other changed file (add-buffer.lua line 62) now enforces a hardcoded cap of 1000 spans. The two changed files disagree on what the segment span limit is: the Lua cap (1000) is not the declared `max_segment_spans`, and the buffer no longer applies the declared limit at all. If `max_segment_spans` is configured below 1000 (or below the Lua cap), oversized segments that this code used to skip will now be flushed. Reconcile the constant: either keep/restore the buffer-side guard against `self.max_segment_spans`, or make the Lua cap derive from the same limit instead of hardcoding 1000.

Make the Lua cap and the Python constant agree — either pass max_segment_spans in as an ARGV instead of the literal 1000, or update the declared constant to 1000 — so the buffer's enforced bound matches the value it declares.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: After taking the write lock, the cache is not checked again. WHY: Concurrent callers that all saw a nil cache each re-read and re-parse the manifest one after another, so a cold start causes a thundering herd of redundant file I/O under an exclusive lock. issues.descricao: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent callers that missed the cache each reload the assets manifest.
issues.textoGolden: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The exclusive lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the blocking file read / synchronous CDN HTTP request (lines 56-67) and there is no re-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. WHY: On a cold cache, all concurrent callers (api/index.go:82, api/frontendsettings.go:62, middleware/recovery.go:141) block on the write lock and then each sequentially re-executes the full load (file I/O or blocking http.DefaultClient.Do), producing a thundering-herd serialization and N redundant loads instead of one; in Dev mode this happens on every request since the fast path is skipped, serializing all concurrent page loads. HOW: after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` re-check the cache (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`) so only the first goroutine performs the load, and drop the defer in favor of releasing the lock immediately after assigning `entryPointAssetsCache = result` to avoid holding it during I/O.

The cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent production requests that initially observe a nil cache each reload and decode the manifest even after another request has populated it. During a cold-start request burst, these redundant filesystem reads and JSON decodes execute serially under the global lock, delaying queued page and frontend-settings requests and blocking cache readers while each reload runs. After acquiring the write lock, return the populated cache when cfg.Env != setting.Dev before performing asset loading.

issues.descricao: GetWebAssets holds a global exclusive mutex through the whole manifest load, so in Dev mode, where the cache is bypassed, every request serializes behind it.
